doc.title: Evan Christopher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 1, 2009

chapter: Hurricane Katrina and New Orleans today
title: Why the federal government owes New Orleans: levees, contracts and cynicism
summary: Asked about people who object to paying for rebuilding, he blames federal levee failures and neglected wetlands. He also criticizes no-bid rebuilding contracts and immigration policy after the storm.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: What would you say to people who take the attitude why are people living there and why should we as a government pay to make it possible for them to live in the same place again?

Well I mean there’s a lot of things you would say. I mean for one thing it’s the government’s fault that the flooding happened to begin with. It was the failure of the federal levies that caused the flooding. Yes, there was a hurricane involved. And there was some wind damage. But the flooding happened because of breaches in the federal levy system. Not just one or two breaches but double digits. I mean there were places where the levies were compromised because they hadn’t been built correctly to begin with. And the Army Corps of Engineers, that’s not locals from New Orleans, it’s not knowing how to build a levy. That’s the federal government. And that’s also the federal government not protecting the wetlands of the Gulf Coast, not holding the businesses and the oil companies and the gas fields more accountable for protecting the natural barrier that exists on the Gulf Coast. So for one thing there’s some accountability of which people need to be reminded. The second thing is that I don’t fault people for not having an understanding about how culturally significant, or economically significant, New Orleans is. People don’t necessarily realize how much commerce comes up from the Gulf into the Mississippi River. That barge traffic, or that barges are still the cheapest way to transport large amounts of goods for imports and exports of sugar, rice, grain, steel. I mean it’s still the cheapest way to move these products. I don’t expect people to know that. I also don’t not understand people’s view, a more cynical view, of just how some spending is not, spending in this country is not done well, especially when it comes to kind of development things. I mean I can understand the cynicism that develops. I mean I became cynical too to find out that two things that happen when you have a situation like this is that the government can give no bid contracts, they can give the contracts for rebuilding to whoever they want, and it’s no coincidence that they went to subsidiaries for Halliburton — Smith, Root & Brown — and other local companies that were basically very key for electing officials in the Republican administration. There is also something where they can really make it easier for immigration policies in this time of emergency. So I can understand how people would be very cynical about, you know, all of a sudden, what happened? How come there’s all of a sudden this huge influx of people from Mexico, El Salvador, Columbia, Central America you know, coming in and not having to go through the same process of people who are legally trying to get here and all of a sudden you’ve got this huge workforce that’s replacing people who theoretically
